rationale: A wins because it keeps the founder out of trouble: it names real proof gates before letting an angle leave the building, especially "the pharmacy chain's name — without it this angle cannot be pitched at all." B has the same basic four shapes, but it gets too cute with unsupported premises like "testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores." That's not an angle; that's an invented experiment wearing a headline hat.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker was the canonical example of that thesis" is outside the supplied update. It may be true, but this exercise required grounding in the fact block, not brand-history muscle memory.
"Warby Parker's founding pitch was eliminating the middleman" is also imported context. If that frame matters, the set should flag it as a claim to verify, not treat it as supplied fact.

"a newly profitable public company is funding a 40-store buildout" overreads the facts. The update says Warby recently reached profitability and is opening stores; it does not say profitability is funding the expansion.
"pharmacy chains' fight to reinvent the front of store" is a real-looking trend peg, but it was not supplied. Source it or cut it.
gaps_in_B: "Warby Parker bets its future on the stores it was built to disrupt" overstates the update. Forty new stores is meaningful; "bets its future" is boardroom fan fiction unless the company said it.
"testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores" invents a comparison the facts do not support. The pilot is a channel test, not a better-than-owned-stores test.
"made its name proving glasses didn't need a showroom" and "built to disrupt" import unsourced brand history and add cliché varnish. The DTC reversal angle works without the TED Talk fog machine.

"the profitability claim and the exam-revenue rollout are being announced together" assumes announcement packaging not in the fact block. The safer version is that both facts are present in the update and create a disclosure question.
